noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: understand how ionisation energies are influenced by the number of protons in the nucleus, the electron shielding and the sub-shell from which the electron is removed
understand reasons for the trend in ionisation energy down Groups 1 and 2

primer.text: First ionisation energy measures the pull a gaseous atom exerts on its outermost electron. Across period 2 or 3 the general trend climbs as nuclear charge rises, radius shrinks and shielding stays put, with two small dips where a new subshell opens or pairing begins. Down any group the trend falls because added shells lengthen the nucleus-to-electron distance and thicken shielding. This note maps both directions and the four famous dips.

lessons.title: The climb across a period
lessons.opening: Moving left to right along period 2 or period 3, first ionisation energy climbs a broad staircase. Protons join the nucleus while the new electrons slot into the same outer shell, so attraction strengthens, atoms contract and the outer electron becomes progressively harder to detach. This lesson fixes the three factors behind that climb.
keyPoints: Across a period the nuclear charge rises because protons are added to the nucleus.
The atomic radius falls as the strengthened pull drags the outer shell inward.
Shielding by inner-shell electrons stays roughly level while electrons enter the same shell.
Removing the outer electron therefore costs more energy at every step across a period.
Group 1 metals sit low on the plot while noble gases reach the highest values.

low.restatement: As you cross a period, atoms keep adding protons and outer electrons to the same shell, so the pull grows, the atom shrinks and the first electron costs more to remove.
low.analogy: Picture a magnet under a sheet of paper with iron filings on it: more magnet strength with the paper thickness unchanged lifts every filing harder, just as extra protons grip the same shell more tightly.
low.examPointer: Quote all three factors when explaining the climb - nuclear charge up, radius down, shielding constant - markers look for the trio.

medium.restatement: The cross-period increase in first ionisation energy is a competition the nucleus wins: proton count grows while the added electron joins an already occupied shell, leaving distance and shielding near constant.
medium.analogy: Think of a loan shark raising the interest rate while the repayment schedule stays fixed: the same outer electron faces a stronger demand every step across the period.
medium.examPointer: When a question hands you a plot of values across a period, anchor your explanation on rising nuclear charge with essentially constant shielding - that pairing earns the marks.

check.stem: What is the general trend in first ionisation energy across period 3?

options.text: It rises overall from sodium to argon
options.explanation: Extra protons strengthen the pull on an outer electron that stays in the third shell.

options.text: It falls overall from sodium to argon
options.explanation: Falling values belong to the down-group trend, not the cross-period one.

options.text: It stays flat because shielding rises
options.explanation: Shielding barely moves across a period since electrons join the same shell.

options.text: It doubles at every element
options.explanation: The climb is steady and modest, not a per-step doubling.

check.stem: Why does the atomic radius shrink as you cross a period?

options.text: Greater nuclear charge pulls the same outer shell closer
options.explanation: More protons attract the electrons in the unchanged shell more strongly.

options.text: Extra inner shells squeeze the atom inward
options.explanation: No new inner shells appear across a period; electrons enter the existing outer shell.

options.text: Electrons pair up and occupy less space
options.explanation: Pairing affects specific dips, not the steady radius contraction.

options.text: The nucleus loses protons by decay
options.explanation: Nuclear decay is irrelevant here; proton count rises across the period.

check.stem: Which quantity stays approximately constant as you cross a period?

options.text: Shielding by inner-shell electrons
options.explanation: The added electron joins the same outer shell, so inner-shell screening barely changes.

options.text: Nuclear charge
options.explanation: Proton count climbs at every element across the period.

options.text: Atomic radius
options.explanation: The radius contracts steadily across the period.

options.text: Number of neutrons in every atom
options.explanation: Neutron counts vary element to element with no shielding role of this kind.

check.stem: Why do noble gases top the first-ionisation-energy plot of their period?

options.text: Their nuclei carry the largest charge of the period acting on a full outer shell
options.explanation: By period's end the proton count is maximal while the shell stays the same, so removal costs the most.

options.text: Their outer electrons orbit faster than other atoms' electrons
options.explanation: Speed plays no part in the electrostatic argument.

options.text: They contain extra inner shells their neighbours lack
options.explanation: Within one period every element has the same number of shells.

options.text: Their atoms are the largest in the period
options.explanation: Noble-gas atoms are actually among the smallest, which is why removal is hardest.

check.stem: Group 1 metals show the lowest first ionisation energies in their periods because

options.text: One distant, well-shielded outer electron is easily lost
options.explanation: A single valence electron sits far from a modestly charged nucleus behind full inner shells.

options.text: Their nuclei contain the fewest protons of any element
options.explanation: Hydrogen and helium are smaller atoms; group 1 is simply low within its own period.

options.text: Their electrons repel the nucleus away
options.explanation: Electron-nucleus repulsion is not part of the model.

options.text: They already have a full outer shell
options.explanation: Group 1 atoms have one outer electron, the opposite of a full shell.

check.stem: State the three changes that explain the general rise in first ionisation energy across a period.
check.modelAnswer: Nuclear charge increases, atomic radius decreases as the outer shell is drawn closer, and shielding by inner-shell electrons stays reasonably constant.

check.stem: Name the two families that bracket the cross-period plot at its lowest and highest points.
check.modelAnswer: Group 1 metals mark the lowest first ionisation energies and the noble gases mark the highest across a period.

check.stem: Explain why shielding barely changes as you travel across a period even though electrons keep being added.
check.modelAnswer: Each new electron joins the same outer shell as the one before it, so the population of inner shells between the nucleus and the outer electron never grows; screening therefore holds near constant across the period.

check.stem: Across period 2 from lithium to neon, identify the element whose atoms have the smallest radius and justify the choice with the cross-period law.
check.modelAnswer: Neon has the smallest radius: by period's end the nucleus carries the period's largest charge while the electrons still occupy the second shell, so the pull draws that shell in most tightly.

lessons.title: The two famous dips
sourceHeadings: Dips in the trend for period 2
Dips in the trend for period 3
lessons.opening: Two kinds of wrinkle interrupt the cross-period climb in both periods 2 and 3: a small drop when the first electron enters a new p subshell, and a second when pairing forces two electrons to share an orbital. Beryllium-to-boron and nitrogen-to-oxygen in period 2 replay as magnesium-to-aluminium and phosphorus-to-sulfur in period 3.
keyPoints: A dip follows beryllium and magnesium because their next electron opens the p subshell, sitting further out than the filled s subshell.
A dip follows nitrogen and phosphorus because each next electron must pair in a p orbital, and spin-pair repulsion eases removal.
Period 2 dips: beryllium 900 to boron 800, nitrogen 1400 to oxygen 1310, in kJ mol^-1.
Period 3 dips: magnesium 738 to aluminium 578, phosphorus 1012 to sulfur 1000, in kJ mol^-1.
The dip mechanism is subshell geometry, not any change in shielding or nuclear charge.

low.restatement: Two spots in each period break the climb: starting a p subshell costs less than expected, and doubling up in a p orbital invites repulsion that helps the electron leave.
low.analogy: Moving into a new office floor takes less effort than squeezing a second colleague into an already occupied desk - the paired-up worker is the first to quit.
low.examPointer: Name the mechanism for each dip type separately: subshell distance for Be-B and Mg-Al, spin-pair repulsion for N-O and P-S.

medium.restatement: The dips are electronic-structure fingerprints: a 2p or 3p electron is higher in energy than a filled s subshell, and a paired p electron adds mutual repulsion, so either way the measured ionisation energy lands below the neighbour before it.
medium.analogy: A commuter penalty: changing trains (new subshell) or sharing a cramped seat (paired orbital) both make the journey easier to abandon than the smooth run before it.
medium.examPointer: Configurations win marks: quote 1s2 2s2 for beryllium against 1s2 2s2 2px1 for boron when explaining that dip.

check.stem: Why does first ionisation energy drop between beryllium and boron?

options.text: Boron's fifth electron enters the 2p subshell, further out than beryllium's filled 2s
options.explanation: A 2p electron is higher in energy and more easily removed than a 2s electron.

options.text: Boron has more inner shells than beryllium
options.explanation: Both atoms keep the same two shells; only the subshell changes.

options.text: Boron's nucleus carries a smaller charge
options.explanation: Proton count rises from beryllium to boron.

options.text: Beryllium's electrons pair up and repel
options.explanation: Beryllium's 2s electrons are already paired and it still shows the higher value; the dip belongs to boron's new subshell.

check.stem: Which effect explains the fall from nitrogen to oxygen?

options.text: Spin-pair repulsion in the newly paired 2p orbital
options.explanation: Two electrons sharing the 2p orbital repel, so one leaves more readily.

options.text: Oxygen's electron entering a further subshell
options.explanation: Oxygen adds no new subshell; it pairs within 2p.

options.text: A sudden fall in nuclear charge
options.explanation: Oxygen's nucleus holds one more proton than nitrogen's.

options.text: Loss of shielding by inner electrons
options.explanation: Inner-shell shielding is unchanged between the two atoms.

check.stem: Using the quoted values, which period-3 dip is numerically the smaller fall in first ionisation energy?

options.text: Phosphorus to sulfur, a 12 kJ mol^-1 fall
options.explanation: 1012 minus 1000 is 12, far below the 160 at magnesium-to-aluminium.

options.text: Magnesium to aluminium, a 160 kJ mol^-1 fall
options.explanation: 738 minus 578 is indeed 160, but that is the larger of the two period-3 dips.

options.text: Both dips are identical at 160 kJ mol^-1
options.explanation: The pairing dip is an order of magnitude smaller than the subshell dip.

options.text: Neither pair dips; both rise
options.explanation: Both famous pairs fall despite rising nuclear charge.

check.stem: The period-2 dip from beryllium to boron measures 100 kJ mol^-1. What is the corresponding nitrogen-to-oxygen dip with values 1400 and 1310 kJ mol^-1?

options.text: 90 kJ mol^-1
options.explanation: 1400 minus 1310 leaves 90 kJ mol^-1.

options.text: 100 kJ mol^-1
options.explanation: That is the beryllium-to-boron dip, not this pair.

options.text: 190 kJ mol^-1
options.explanation: Adding the values instead of subtracting invents a larger fall.

options.text: 110 kJ mol^-1
options.explanation: No subtraction of the quoted pair yields 110.

check.stem: In period 3, which electron configuration change starts the subshell dip?

options.text: Aluminium's thirteenth electron opening the 3p subshell
options.explanation: A 3p electron sits further from the nucleus than magnesium's filled 3s, so removal is easier.

options.text: Sulfur pairing its 3p electrons
options.explanation: Pairing drives the phosphorus-to-sulfur dip, the other mechanism.

options.text: Magnesium losing its 3s electrons
options.explanation: Magnesium keeps its 3s pair; the dip appears at aluminium.

options.text: Silicon promoting an electron into 3d
options.explanation: No 3d electrons appear in these ground-state configurations.

check.stem: State the two mechanisms that produce the dips in the cross-period trend, with one element pair for each.
check.modelAnswer: A new p subshell opening causes the beryllium-to-boron dip (and magnesium-to-aluminium), while spin-pair repulsion causes the nitrogen-to-oxygen dip (and phosphorus-to-sulfur).

check.stem: Quote the four first-ionisation-energy pairs that define the dips of periods 2 and 3, in kJ mol^-1.
check.modelAnswer: Beryllium 900 to boron 800, nitrogen 1400 to oxygen 1310, magnesium 738 to aluminium 578, and phosphorus 1012 to sulfur 1000.

check.stem: A student argues the nitrogen-to-oxygen dip shows oxygen's nucleus is weaker. Explain why that reading fails.
check.modelAnswer: Oxygen's nucleus actually holds one more proton than nitrogen's; the fall arises because the added electron must share a 2p orbital, and the resulting spin-pair repulsion makes that paired electron cheaper to remove than an unpaired one.

check.stem: Taking the four quoted dips, calculate each fall in kJ mol^-1 and rank them from largest to smallest.
check.modelAnswer: Beryllium-to-boron falls 100, nitrogen-to-oxygen falls 90, magnesium-to-aluminium falls 160, phosphorus-to-sulfur falls 12; ranked largest to smallest: Mg-Al 160, Be-B 100, N-O 90, P-S 12.

lessons.title: The slide down a group
sourceHeadings: Summary Explanation for Trend in Ionisation Energy Across a Period and Down a Group
lessons.opening: Descend any group and first ionisation energy falls at every step. The nucleus gains protons, yet each new element wraps its outer electron in an extra shell: the electron stands further away behind thicker shielding, and those two effects swamp the extra charge. This lesson assembles the full four-factor argument.
keyPoints: First ionisation energy decreases down a group.
Nuclear charge rises down a group as protons are added.
Atomic radius grows because each element down the group adds a shell of electrons.
The nucleus-to-outer-electron distance and the shielding both increase down the group.
The distance and shielding gains outweigh the extra nuclear charge, easing removal.

low.restatement: Going down a column, the outer electron sits on a further-out shell behind more screening, so it leaves more easily even though the nucleus is more charged.
low.analogy: A whisper from the front of a hall barely reaches the back rows: extra rows (shells) and more people in front (shielding) drown out the louder voice (extra protons).
low.examPointer: Always concede the rising nuclear charge before overruling it with distance and shielding - answers that skip the concession lose marks.

medium.restatement: Down-group decline is a weighted sum: proton count adds attraction, but an extra shell adds distance and screening, and the product of those two dominates the electrostatic balance that binds the outer electron.
medium.analogy: Two friends pulling a rope towards you versus the rope getting longer and a colleague leaning on the middle: length plus slack beats the extra puller.
medium.examPointer: For 'explain the trend down group 2' style questions, order the argument: charge up, radius and distance up, shielding up, therefore removal easier.

check.stem: What happens to first ionisation energy on descending group 2 from beryllium to barium?

options.text: It decreases at each step
options.explanation: Added shells push the outer electron further out behind more shielding.

options.text: It increases because nuclei gain protons
options.explanation: The proton gain is overruled by distance and shielding.

options.text: It stays constant within a group
options.explanation: Values fall steadily down the column.

options.text: It alternates up and down
options.explanation: No zigzag appears down a main group.

check.stem: Which pair of effects overrules the rising nuclear charge down a group?

options.text: Greater atomic radius with heavier shielding
options.explanation: A longer nucleus-to-electron distance behind more inner shells wins the balance.

options.text: Falling nuclear charge with stable shielding
options.explanation: Nuclear charge rises down the group; shielding rises too.

options.text: Shrinking radius with growing shielding
options.explanation: The radius grows down a group, it does not shrink.

options.text: Electron affinity of the element below
options.explanation: Electron affinity is a different quantity altogether.

check.stem: Down a group, what happens to the separation between an atom's nucleus and its outermost electron?

options.text: It increases because extra shells are added
options.explanation: Every new period wraps the outer electron one shell further out.

options.text: It decreases as charge pulls the shell in
options.explanation: Within a group the shell count grows rather than the charge pulling harder.

options.text: It remains fixed for the whole group
options.explanation: Distance plainly grows with shell count.

options.text: It first rises then falls
options.explanation: The increase is monotonic down the group.

check.stem: Why does adding protons down a group fail to raise the ionisation energy?

options.text: The outer electron is both further away and better screened from the extra charge
options.explanation: Distance and shielding blunt the additional attraction before it reaches the outer electron.

options.text: The added protons sit outside the nucleus
options.explanation: Protons always reside in the nucleus.

options.text: Extra protons convert to neutrons down the group
options.explanation: Proton number defines the element and keeps rising.

options.text: Electrons move at constant speed regardless of charge
options.explanation: Speed is not part of the electrostatic argument.

check.stem: Group 1 members lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium and caesium stand in charge order. Which atom holds its outer electron most tightly?

options.text: Lithium, the smallest member of the group
options.explanation: Fewest shells means shortest distance and least shielding, so removal costs most.

options.text: Caesium, the most charged member
options.explanation: Its extra charge is swamped by five shells of shielding.

options.text: Potassium, the middle member
options.explanation: The trend is monotonic; no mid-group turnaround.

options.text: All five bind equally
options.explanation: The values fall continuously down the group.

check.stem: State the down-group trend in first ionisation energy and the two effects that dominate it.
check.modelAnswer: First ionisation energy decreases down a group because increasing atomic radius and increasing shielding outweigh the rising nuclear charge.

check.stem: List the four factor changes used in the standard down-group explanation, in the order they are usually argued.
check.modelAnswer: Nuclear charge increases, atomic radius increases, nucleus-to-electron distance increases, shielding increases - and the latter outweigh the first.

check.stem: Explain why the increasing nuclear charge down a group cannot rescue the falling ionisation energy.
check.modelAnswer: Each step down the group adds a whole shell of electrons, so the outer electron ends up further from the nucleus and behind more inner-shell screening; the attractive grip per electron falls even while total charge rises.

check.stem: Using the down-group law only, arrange lithium, caesium, potassium and sodium in order of decreasing first ionisation energy and give the reason at the first step.
check.modelAnswer: Lithium > sodium > potassium > caesium: lithium's outer electron occupies the fewest shells, sitting closest to its nucleus behind the least shielding, so it is the hardest to remove.

glossary.definition: The energy needed to remove one outer electron from each gaseous atom of an element, quoted in kJ mol^-1.
The screening of the outer electron from nuclear attraction by inner-shell electrons.
The extra repulsion between the two electrons sharing one orbital, which eases removal of a paired electron.
The repeating pattern of chemical and physical properties shown by elements across the periods of the periodic table.
